description_full: Compañía de Minas Buenaventura S.A.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the exploration, development, construction, and operation of mines in Peru, the Americas, Europe, and Asia. It explores for gold, silver, copper, zinc, lead, and antimony deposits. The company also engages in the exploration, extraction, concentration, smelting, and marketing of polymetallic minerals and metals. In addition, it is involved in electricity transmission and generation; hydroelectric plant operation; and production of manganese sulfate monohydrate, as well as tailings dam management. The company was incorporated in 1953 and is based in Lima, Peru.

financial_summary: Buenaventura Mining Company Inc is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $6.3B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +5.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at -2% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $148M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.17× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 6.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.4%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 29% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 44% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 53% and a beta of 0.74, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.19 vs 5y 0.55), so read it loosely.
About $27.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $18.84 (margin of safety -32%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.75 to $24.77 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on P/E 5.3 vs 16.3 and EV/EBITDA 5.0 vs 8.3, richer on P/FCF 42.5 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $38.00 on average, 53% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 11.2% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 4.03).
It runs a 11% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.17x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).

hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.6% over 3 years and 11.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
Free cash flow has compounded 23.6% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 44.2% on average.
Analysts expect -14.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 28.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 60%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.4% (4.6% in dividends).
